draft.title: Mutually exclusive events and the addition rule
card: \(P(A \text{ or } B)\) is the chance that \(A\) happens, or \(B\) happens, or both. The rule is \(P(A \text{ or } B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \text{ and } B)\).
We subtract \(P(A \text{ and } B)\) because outcomes in both \(A\) and \(B\) are counted twice when we add \(P(A)\) and \(P(B)\).
Mutually exclusive events cannot happen together, so \(P(A \text{ and } B) = 0\). Then \(P(A \text{ or } B) = P(A) + P(B)\).
draft.remember: Add the two chances, then take away the overlap so it is counted once.

a.q: Suppose \(P(A) = 0.6\), \(P(B) = 0.3\) and \(P(A \text{ and } B) = 0.1\). Find \(P(A \text{ or } B)\).
a.why: \(P(A \text{ or } B) = 0.6 + 0.3 - 0.1 = 0.8\). Adding only \(P(A)\) and \(P(B)\) gives 0.9, which counts the overlap twice.

b.q: At a school in Parramatta, the chance a student plays netball is 0.35 and the chance a student plays chess is 0.15. No student does both. What is the chance a student plays netball or chess?
b.why: No student does both, so the events are mutually exclusive and \(P(A \text{ and } B) = 0\). Then \(P(A \text{ or } B) = 0.35 + 0.15 = 0.50\). The product 0.0525 is not used here, because the rule adds the chances.
b.clue: If no one does both, what is the overlap?

problems.detail: Why (b) writes P(A and B) and P(A or B) without saying that A is netball and B is chess. The question never names events A and B, so the link may confuse some students.
